introduction-to-economics: Even the richest person on Earth cannot have everything. Why not?
When economists disagree, is it about the evidence or about values?
What four kinds of resources go into making even a simple loaf of bread?
Who decides what gets made: prices, planners or a mix of the two?
microeconomics: Why do economists insist that a price cut does not increase demand?
Why do farmers grow more when prices rise, and what makes them grow less at every price?
How can a change in one market move prices in a completely different one?
macroeconomics: If a country's output is worth more money this year, has it really produced more?
How can one number tell you how much prices have risen for a whole country of shoppers?
Can a country's income tell you how well its people really live?
Why does an economy grow in bursts and slumps instead of at a steady pace?
Two countries earn the same income per person. How can one be far more developed?
the-global-economy: Why do countries buy from abroad things they could make perfectly well at home?
Why did the world start trading so much more, and does everyone come out ahead?
When a country taxes goods from abroad, who ends up paying, and who comes out ahead?
If trade makes a country richer overall, why do so many governments still choose to restrict it?
Why would a country give up control over its own trade rules to join a club of its neighbours?
Why would a country give up its own money, and what does it lose by doing so?
aggregate-demand-supply: If every price in a country goes up at once, why would people buy less of the country's output?
What makes a whole country suddenly stop spending, even when pay has not changed?
Why does business spending on new machines and buildings swing so much more than household spending?
Why can a jump in oil prices make a whole economy produce less and charge more at once?
What sets the most a country can produce, and can extra spending push past it?
Why can prices and unemployment rise at the same time?
If a slump ends by itself, why do some economists say we should not wait?
competitive-market-equilibrium: When a price is too high or too low, what pulls it back to where buyers and sellers agree?
When a harvest fails or buyers rush in, which way do prices move, and how far?
With no one in charge, how do millions of buyers and sellers end up producing what people want?
When you would gladly pay more than the price, where does that extra value go?
If buyers and sellers both gain from a trade, how can a free market still produce the wrong amount?
economics-inequality-poverty: If almost everyone in a country gets richer, can more people end up counted as poor?
Can a tax take more money from richer people and still hit poorer people harder?
Why can a pay rise leave a low-income family barely any better off?
elasticity-demand: Why do some buyers barely react when a price jumps, while others switch away at once?
When a seller charges more, why does the money coming in sometimes go up and sometimes go down?
When people get richer, why do they buy less of some things?
When prices jump, why can some producers flood the market while others cannot grow more for years?
exchange-rates: Nobody sets the price of a dollar or a euro, so what decides it from one day to the next?
Why can one decision by a central bank change what a currency is worth around the world?
Can a country choose the price of its own money, and what does it cost to try?
When a country's money loses value abroad, who wins and who loses at home?
When a country buys more from the world than it sells, how does it pay the difference?
externalities-common-pool-resources: Why does a factory that pays all its own bills still produce too much?
When a product harms people nearby who never bought it, why does the market sell too much?
Why do fishers who all want fish next year still empty the sea this year?
How can a government put a price on cleaner air before deciding whether to build a road?
macroeconomic-objectives: Can an economy keep growing just by people spending more?
Who counts as unemployed, and who slips through the count?
Why are some people out of work even when the economy is booming?
If a law lifts the lowest pay, do some workers lose their jobs?
What makes prices across a whole economy keep going up?
If all pay rose as fast as prices, would inflation still hurt anyone?
Why can't a government get fast growth, plenty of jobs and steady prices all at once?
monetary-policy: How can one interest rate, set by a handful of people, slow down inflation across a whole country?
If your savings grow every year, how can you still end up able to buy less?
When a slump hits, can a government spend its way out of it?
If a country's yearly deficit keeps shrinking, how can its debt still be growing?
How can a government raise the most its economy can produce, and why does it take so long?
Should a country's trains, water pipes and power lines be run by the state or by private companies?
role-government: What happens when a government makes something cheaper by law?
Why would a government ever make something cost more?
When a government taxes sugary drinks, who really pays the tax: the shoppers or the companies?
When a government pays firms for every item they make, who ends up with the money?
role-government-part-2: If everyone gains from a lighthouse, why might no one choose to pay for it?
If a vaccine also protects the people around you, why might too few people get one?
Should a government tax pollution, ban it, or let firms buy and sell the right to pollute?
When a government steps in to fix a market, how can it end up making things worse?
sustainable-development: Can a country get richer today in a way that leaves its future poorer?
Why can a country full of oil, copper or cocoa still stay poor for decades?
When a global company builds a factory in a poorer country, who really gains?
Can opening up to world markets and foreign firms make a poor country richer?
Can a government make a poor country richer by stepping in where markets do too little?
When rich countries give or lend to poorer ones, when does it actually help them grow?
what-is-economics-part-2: Why does each extra unit of one thing cost a country more and more of another?
Why must a country's total spending, total income and total output always be equal?
How can you sum up who gets what in a whole country with a single number?
Should governments leave markets alone? Why have great economists given such different answers?
